Whether you're buying, building, or dealing with a problem, a surveyor can give you the facts you need to make a sound decision. We introduce you to a suitable UK surveyor who will quote you directly, with prices on application.
need_heading: What people searching for surveyors usually need
need_lead: A surveyor can help in many property situations, and knowing which type you need is the first step.
needs: You're buying a home and want a condition report before you commit, so you know what repairs might lie ahead.
You're planning an extension or conversion and need advice on whether the structure can take the work.
You're selling and a buyer's survey has raised issues that you want to understand and respond to.
You're dealing with a party wall matter and need a surveyor who specialises in those disputes.
You need a valuation for probate, matrimonial or other legal purposes, and want an independent figure.
context_heading: Understanding surveyors and how to choose
context: Surveyors work across many specialisms, from residential condition reports to commercial valuation and party wall matters. Many are members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), and RICS-regulated firms must follow professional standards, hold insurance and offer a complaints process. Chartered surveyors use the letters MRICS or FRICS after their name, which shows they have met RICS's qualifications.

For specialist work, check for the relevant body: for example, the Faculty of Party Wall Surveyors for party wall matters, or the Property Care Association for damp and timber specialists. For asbestos surveys, look for organisations accredited by UKAS. It's also worth asking which report type you are getting and confirming the surveyor is independent of the sale.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Tell us the type of property or land involved, such as a house, flat, or commercial building, and its approximate age.
Explain the purpose of the survey, for example buying, building, valuing, or resolving a dispute.
Mention any specific concerns, such as damp, structural movement, or party wall issues.
Let us know if you have a deadline, such as a mortgage offer expiry or exchange date.
Say whether you need a particular type of surveyor, such as a chartered surveyor or a party wall specialist.
Tell us your location and the property's location, so we can introduce you to a surveyor who covers that area.
questions: Are you a member of RICS, and what do the letters after your name mean?
Which type of survey report do you recommend for this property, and what does it include?
Will you be independent of the sale, and do you have any connection to the seller or agent?
How do you handle complaints if I'm unhappy with the report?
What is your experience with properties like mine, and do you have specialist knowledge for my concern?
Can you confirm your professional indemnity insurance covers this work?

faqs.q: Do I need a surveyor if I'm buying a home?
faqs.a: It's wise to have a survey before you commit, as it can reveal issues that aren't obvious. A surveyor can report on condition and highlight repairs, helping you decide whether to proceed or renegotiate.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a valuation and a survey?
faqs.a: A valuation is typically for mortgage purposes and gives the lender a figure, while a survey is a more detailed inspection of condition. If you need both, ask whether they can be combined.

faqs.q: How do I check a surveyor's credentials?
faqs.a: Many surveyors are members of RICS, and you can check the RICS directory. For specialist work, look for membership of the relevant body, such as the Faculty of Party Wall Surveyors or the Property Care Association.

faqs.q: Can iComply recommend a surveyor near me?
faqs.a: We introduce you to a suitable UK surveyor based on your needs and location. They will then quote you directly, with prices on application, and you can decide whether to proceed.

extra_heading: Comparing several surveyors before you choose
extra: Searching for surveyors in the plural suggests you are weighing up more than one option rather than taking the first name you come across. That is a sensible instinct, because surveying covers a wide range of work and two practices may offer quite different things depending on their specialisms and the type of report they produce. Knowing what to compare makes the choice much clearer.

Ask each surveyor which report they are proposing and what it covers, since a condition report, a homebuyer-style survey and a full building survey are not the same thing. Check whether they are members of RICS and what the letters after their name indicate, and confirm that they are independent of the sale. For specialist concerns such as damp, timber or party wall matters, ask whether they hold membership of the relevant body for that work.

Price matters, but compare like with like: a lower fee for a less detailed report is not really a saving if it leaves you without the answers you need. Ask what the quote includes, whether the surveyor will discuss findings with you afterwards, and what their complaints process is. Once you have those answers side by side, the right surveyor for your situation usually becomes obvious.

extra_faqs.q: Why would I approach several surveyors rather than just one?
extra_faqs.a: Different practices specialise in different areas, and the type of report you are offered can vary. Comparing a few lets you weigh up what is included, whether the surveyor is independent of the sale, and how clearly they explain their findings before you commit.

extra_faqs.q: Is a cheaper quote always better value?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily, because a lower fee may reflect a less detailed report or a narrower scope. Ask what the quote covers and whether the surveyor will talk you through the results, so you can judge value rather than price alone.

extra_faqs.q: Can I ask a surveyor about a specific worry before instructing them?
extra_faqs.a: Yes, and it is worth doing. Describing your concern, such as damp, structural movement or a party wall issue, lets the surveyor tell you whether they handle that kind of work or whether you need a specialist instead.
